spans.content: Effects of Nitrogen on the Microstructure and Mechanical
Properties of Fe–28Mn–10Al–0.8C Low-Density Steel
Shuai Guo, Hangyu Zhu,* Jixuan Zhao, Mingming Song, Jianli Li, and Zhengliang Xue
Herein, the relationships among nitrogen content, inclusion characteristics,
microstructure, and mechanical properties of low-density steel are investigated.
The austenite grain size is refined with nitrogen addition to the low-density steel,
and the ultimate tensile strength, plasticity, fracture toughness, and impact
toughness are distinctly enhanced. However, the yield strength decreases due to
a decrease in the ferrite content with nitrogen addition. AlN is determined to be
the main inclusion in the high-nitrogen low-density steel, and the number
percentage of AlN that is less than 2 μm reaches 84%, which promotes the
refinement of austenite grains. In addition, aggregated AlN inclusions in the
dimples of the steel are observed, which are generated during the smelting
process, and the aggregated AlN inclusions tend to cause crack initiation in the
low-density steel.

2. Experimental Section
2.1. Materials Preparation
Low-density steels with a chemical composition of Fe-28 wt%
Mn-10 wt% Al-0.8 wt% C and different nitrogen contents were
used to investigate the effects of nitrogen on their microstructure
and mechanical properties. The raw materials for the steels
included pure iron, ferromanganese, carbon particles, aluminum
particles, and manganese nitrogen alloy. Ingots (50 kg) of low-
density steel were manufactured using a vacuum medium-
frequency induction furnace. The chemical compositions of
the low-density steels are listed in . The ingots were held
at 1423 K for 2 h and then multidirectionally hot forged in a
temperature range of 1123–1323 K, followed by air cooling.

The mechanical properties of the investigated low-density steels
are presented in and , which show that the values
<sup>Figure 2 Table 2</sup>of UTS for the low-nitrogen (LN) and high-nitrogen (HN) steels

4. Discussion
4.1. Effects of Nitrogen on Inclusions
The addition of nitrogen promoted the formation of AlN in the low-
density steels investigated in this study. The formation of AlN inclu
sions was mainly controlled by the reaction equilibrium based on Al
and N content, temperature, Gibbs free energy, activity coefficients,
and interaction coefficients. Based on the calculation method
reported in our previous work,<sup>[22]</sup> an AlN stability diagram of
Figure 8. AlN stability diagram of Fe–28Mn–10Al–0.8C steels.
Fe–28Mn–10Al–0.8C steels was calculated and is presented as
. In addition, the liquidus (1587 K) and solidus (1493 K)
of the investigated steel were calculated using FactSage 8.0. The
Al and N contents of the LN and HN steels are also indicated in
Figure 8, which can be used to examine the formation of AlN inclu-
sions (i.e., by comparison with the stability diagram). For LN steel, the
composition of Al and N fell below the equilibrium line of the smelt-
ing temperature, which suggests that AlN was not a stable phase and
could not be generated during the smelting process. However, for
HN steel with 0.1326 wt% nitrogen, the composition far exceeded
the equilibrium line. The results indicate that AlN inclusions can
be easily formed and stably exist during the smelting process.
In general, AlN inclusions are generated during the solidifica-
tion process with lower Al and N contents and can be formed in
molten steel with higher Al and N contents. Alba et al.<sup>[20]</sup> con-
cluded that the main inclusion was AlN–MnS inclusion in
Fe–5Mn–3Al steel, whereas the nitrogen content was less than
10 ppm. With an increase in N content, AlN became the domi-
nant inclusion. The results coincided with those observed in the
current work, as shown in Figure 4–7.
4.2. Effects of Nitrogen on Microstructure
To clarify the effects of nitrogen content on the microstructure of
low-density steel, a pseudobinary phase diagram of the Fe–
28Mn–10Al–0.8C–N system was calculated using Thermo-Calc
software based on the TCFE8 database (see ). The figure
<sup>Figure 9</sup>shows that the maximum formation temperature and tempera-
ture range of the austenite phase increased significantly and that
ferrite gradually disappeared with the increase in nitrogen con-
tent in the steel. As a stabilizing element for austenite, nitrogen
expanded the austenite phase area and promoted the growth of
the austenite nucleus, thereby preventing the growth of ferrite.
As shown in Figure 3, a large number of annealing twins were
observed between the austenite grains, which crossed each other
and cut the matrix to refine the grains.<sup>[24]</sup>

between the HN and LN steels were associated with the AlN

and AlN inclusions were formed during the smelting process
for the HN steel. The fine AlN inclusions acted as the cores

cation process.<sup>[26]</sup> In addition, Li et al.<sup>[27,28]</sup> reported that some
fine and dispersed inclusions could effectively pin the austenite

4.3. Effects of Nitrogen on Mechanical Properties
Researchers have confirmed that steel with fine grains has excel-
lent strength, plasticity, and toughness.<sup>[11–18,28]</sup> The results of the
tensile tests in the present study were consistent with those from
the literatures, as indicated in Table 2 and Figure 2. The results
showed that the plasticity of the HN steel was obviously better
than that of the LN steel, and the LN steel generally broke earlier
than the HN steel during local necking. Hans and Roylance
et al.<sup>[29,30]</sup> reported that the areas under stress–strain curves
can represent the rated energy consumed by the fracture metal
materials. According to the theory, the energy consumption of
HN steel fracture is higher than that of LN steel. shows
<sup>Figure 10</sup>the morphologies of the tensile fractures of the LN and HN
steels. The macroscopic necking degree of the HN steel was con-
siderably greater than that of the LN steel. Large dimples were
observed in the fractures of the HN steel, which was usually sur-
rounded by small dimples. The dimples in the LN steel were
smaller in size and greater in number, which indicated that
the local stress concentration of the LN steel was more severe
during the deformation process. The HN steel was larger and
had a deeper depth and more uniform distribution of dimples,
which suggested that the plasticity and toughness were
improved.<sup>[31]</sup> The improved plasticity and fracture toughness
in the HN steel was due to the fine grains, and many twins
caused the deformation to become more uniform and relieve
the stress concentration of the deformed steel matrix. In addi-
tion, many grain and twin boundaries prevented crack propaga-
tion and enhanced fracture toughness.<sup>[32,33]</sup> Griffith’s equation
describes the effect of grain refinement on toughness, as shown
in the following equation.<sup>[28]</sup>

than that of the LN steel, and the LN steel generally broke earlier
than the HN steel during local necking. Hans and Roylance

materials. According to the theory, the energy consumption of
HN steel fracture is higher than that of LN steel. shows

Finally, the changes in the number and sizes of inclusions
derived from nitrogen addition also had obvious effects on the
mechanical properties of the HN steel. Different types of inclu-
sions were detected in the dimples on the fracture surfaces of the
test samples, as shown in , indicating that these inclu-
sions became the initial point of fracture. The sulfide inclusions
showed good deformation ability and were typically large; how-
ever, these sulfide inclusions could easily break away from cracks
at the inclusion–matrix interface due to their weak binding force
to the steel matrix.<sup>[38,39]</sup> In comparison, the brittle AlN inclusions
had a high melting point and exhibited poor deformation ability.
For HN steel, fine and dispersed AlN inclusions could refine the
austenite grains and improve their mechanical properties.

However, aggregated AlN inclusions were detected in the HN
steel (see Figure 12b), which could deteriorate the steel proper-

5. Conclusion
In this study, the effects of nitrogen on the non-metallic
inclusions, microstructure, and mechanical properties of
Fe-28Mn-10Al-0.8C low-density steel were investigated. The
following conclusions were drawn. 1) Nitrogen addition signifi-
cantly decreased the grain size and increased the grain number
and austenite content, which improved the UTS, plasticity, frac-
ture toughness, and impact toughness of low-density steels.
However, the YS decreased with a decrease in the ferrite content
with nitrogen addition. 2) The main inclusions in the LN steel
were AlN, sulfide, and their compound inclusions. The dominant
inclusion in the HN steel was AlN, and the NP of AlN less than
2 μm in size in the HN steel reached 84%. The fine and dispersed
AlN inclusions that were small in size could refine the austenite
grains, which is beneficial to plasticity and toughness.
3) Aggregated AlN inclusions were detected in the dimples of
the HN steel that were generated during the smelting process.
The aggregated AlN inclusions were detrimental to the mechan-
ical properties of the low-density steel, which tended to initiate
crack formation.
